Two samples
The original code first fitted the era models with every patient, with a comment that this was done by request, and then kept only patients with four rows and fitted them again. Both are kept here, as a named list of two data frames, so every later step runs on each in a loop. The printed table counts patients by number of rows: two (a RUSH-era visit only) or four (both eras).

Decision pending: which of the two samples produced the P values the article reports for the era comparison is decision issue #2.

# The original code fitted every era model twice (analysis-plan.md 8.6):
# first "by request" with every patient, including those with a RUSH-era
# visit only, and then with the patients who had four rows, a visit in each
# era. A RUSH-era-only patient's two rows inform the RUSH-era change, the
# sum of the post_visit and post_visit:rush_era coefficients; they cannot
# separate the two, but pooled with both-era patients they move the
# estimate of the interaction and its standard error, which is why the two
# samples can give different era P values.
era_samples <- list(
  all_patients = both_eras_long,
  both_eras = both_eras_long |>
    add_count(patient_number, name = "rows_per_patient") |>
    filter(rows_per_patient == rows_per_patient_both_eras) |>
    select(-rows_per_patient)
)
# Patients by rows each, as the original code's "tab NumObs"
both_eras_long |>
  count(patient_number, name = "rows_per_patient") |>
  count(rows_per_patient) |>
  print()

section: Does the pattern differ by characteristic?
text:
Does the pattern differ by characteristic?
Every term of the era model interacted with the characteristic: post_visit * rush_era * gender adds post_visit:genderMale, rush_era:genderMale and post_visit:rush_era:genderMale to the era model, as Stata’s i.Intervention##i.RUSHEra##i.Gender does. Unlike the RUSH-era models, the characteristic’s own main effect is kept. Each era’s rows take sex, age group and race from that era’s sheet, and age group in particular is the age at that era’s visit, years apart, so it can change within a patient; then its main effect is estimable, and leaving it out would fit a different model. Where a characteristic is the same in all of every patient’s rows, clogit() returns its main effect as NA and Stata omits it, with the same result. The joint Wald test of all these interaction terms asks whether any part of the pattern differs by the characteristic, which is what the original code’s testparm lists tested. The original code itself called these models complicated and included them for completeness.
Two models could not be fitted with every patient and are skipped there; with patients from both eras the original code fitted all of them, and so does this version.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Whether any of the era terms differ by a characteristic: every term of
# the era model interacted with it, Stata's
# "i.Intervention##i.RUSHEra##i.<characteristic>", and one joint Wald test
# of all the interaction terms, as the original code's testparm. The
# characteristic's own main effect is kept: each era's rows take the
# characteristic from that era's sheet, so age group, for example, can
# differ between a patient's pre-RUSH and RUSH-era rows, and then the main
# effect is estimable. Where it is constant within every patient, clogit()
# returns it as NA, as Stata omits it. Models the original code could not
# fit with every patient are skipped there (R/setup.R).
era_subgroup_models <- list()
era_subgroup_tests <- list()
for (sample in names(era_samples)) {
  for (subgroup in names(subgroups_era)) {
    for (outcome in names(outcomes)) {
      skipped <- skipped_era_subgroup_models_all |>
        filter(.data$outcome == .env$outcome, .data$subgroup == .env$subgroup)
      if (sample == "all_patients" && nrow(skipped) > 0) {
        next
      }
      model <- fit_conditional_logit(
        era_samples[[sample]],
        outcome,
        str_glue("post_visit * rush_era * {subgroup}")
      )
      era_subgroup_models[[sample]][[subgroup]][[outcome]] <- model
      subgroup_levels <- model$xlevels[[subgroup]]
      era_subgroup_tests[[sample]][[subgroup]][[outcome]] <- wald_test(
        model,
        c(
          interaction_terms("post_visit", subgroup, subgroup_levels),
          interaction_terms("rush_era", subgroup, subgroup_levels),
          interaction_terms("post_visit:rush_era", subgroup, subgroup_levels)
        )
      )
    }
  }
}

title: 5. Comparison with the pre-RUSH era
text:
Random-intercept models
For comparison, the era model with a random intercept per patient, (1 | patient_number), in place of the strata: R’s version of Stata’s xtset PatientNumber and xtlogit. nAGQ = 12 asks for adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature with 12 points, Stata’s default. Unlike the conditional model it also uses differences between patients, and assumes the patient effect is unrelated to the visit and the era (Methodological background). Similar answers from the two kinds of model are reassuring; the article reports the conditional one.


Click to show/hide R Code
# For comparison, the same era model with a random intercept for each
# patient instead of a stratum, the R equivalent of Stata's xtlogit. Unlike
# the conditional model, it also uses the differences between patients, so
# it assumes the random intercept is unrelated to the visit and era.
random_effects_models <- list()
random_effects_effects <- list()
for (sample in names(era_samples)) {
  for (outcome in names(outcomes)) {
    model <- glmer(
      as.formula(str_glue("{outcome} ~ post_visit * rush_era + (1 | patient_number)")),
      data = era_samples[[sample]],
      family = binomial,
      nAGQ = quadrature_points
    )
    random_effects_models[[sample]][[outcome]] <- model
    random_effects_effects[[sample]][[outcome]] <- tidy_odds_ratios(
      model, confidence_level
    )
  }
}

text: References

title: Methodological background
text: This page explains, in general terms, the methods a before-and-after study of a binary outcome rests on. Nothing here is specific to this study; what this study chose is on Study design and methods. The numbers in the examples are invented.

title: Methodological background
text:
Paired binary data
When the same people are measured twice, before and after some event, each person gives a pair of answers. For a yes-or-no outcome there are four kinds of pair:




After: yes
After: no




Before: yes
a
b


Before: no
c
d



The proportion with the outcome before is (a + b)/n, and after is (a + c)/n. Their difference is (c − b)/n: the cells a and d, people whose answer did not change, cancel. All the information about change is in the discordant pairs, b (got worse) and c (got better).
The two measurements are not independent. A person in care before a visit is more likely to be in care after it than a person who was not, whatever the visit did. Treating the before and after groups as two separate samples, for example with a chi-squared test on a 2 × 2 table of period by outcome, ignores this correlation and gives wrong standard errors. Paired methods use each person as their own control.
Example. Of 100 people, 30 had the outcome both times (a), 5 lost it (b), 20 gained it (c) and 45 never had it (d). The proportion rose from 35% to 50%. Only the 25 discordant pairs say anything about change, and 20 of the 25 changed for the better.

title: Methodological background
text:
McNemar’s test
McNemar’s test asks whether the two kinds of discordant pair are equally common, which is the same as asking whether the before and after proportions are equal (McNemar 1947). If change in either direction were equally likely, each discordant pair would be a coin toss, and c would follow a binomial distribution with n = b + c and probability 0.5.

Chi-squared version: (c − b)² / (b + c), compared with a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom. In the example, (20 − 5)² / 25 = 9.0, P = 0.003.
Exact version: the binomial probability of a split as uneven as 20 to 5 or more, in either direction, from 25 tosses: P = 0.004. It is preferred when b + c is small.

Stata’s mcc command reports both. In R, mcnemar.test(table, correct = FALSE) gives the chi-squared version (without the continuity correction, as Stata’s), and binom.test(c, b + c) the exact one.
McNemar’s test gives a P value but no model: it cannot adjust for anything or ask whether the change differs between groups. Conditional logistic regression does both.

title: Methodological background
text:
Conditional logistic regression
Ordinary logistic regression of the outcome on a period indicator, with every observation treated as independent, has the same flaw as the two-sample chi-squared test. One fix would be to add a separate intercept for every person, so that each person’s baseline tendency is allowed for. But with two observations per person that adds as many parameters as there are people, and the estimates are badly biased.
Conditional logistic regression removes the person-specific intercepts instead of estimating them. Within each person, or each stratum, it uses only the probability of the observed pattern of outcomes given how many of that person’s observations had the outcome. That conditional probability does not depend on the person’s intercept, so the intercepts drop out of the likelihood entirely. What remains depends only on terms that change within a person.
Three consequences matter in practice:

Concordant pairs carry no information. A person who had the outcome both times, or neither time, has only one possible pattern given their total, so they contribute nothing. Software keeps them in the data but they do not affect the estimates.
For matched pairs, the odds ratio is c/b. With one binary period term, the conditional maximum-likelihood odds ratio for “after” against “before” is the ratio of the discordant pairs: 20/5 = 4.0 in the example. Its score test is McNemar’s chi-squared test. This is why a paired study can report McNemar’s test and a conditional odds ratio side by side. Software usually reports the model’s Wald test instead, (log OR)² divided by its variance, 1/b + 1/c: in the example (log 4)² / (1/5 + 1/20) = 7.7 against McNemar’s 9.0, P = 0.006 against 0.003. Both test the same hypothesis; they differ more when the discordant pairs are few or very unbalanced.
Characteristics that do not change within a person cannot have a main effect. Sex, race or age group at a visit is the same in both of a person’s observations, so its effect is absorbed into the person’s intercept and removed with it. Stata drops such terms with a note; in R they come back as NA, or are better left out of the formula. This is not a limitation: it is the price of controlling for every stable characteristic, measured or not.

With more than two observations per stratum and several of them having the outcome, the exact conditional likelihood sums over every way the outcomes could have been arranged, which takes more computation. Both Stata’s clogit and R’s survival::clogit(method = "exact") compute it exactly (Therneau, n.d.).

title: Methodological background
section: Does the change differ between groups? Interactions
text:
Does the change differ between groups? Interactions
A characteristic that is the same before and after cannot have a main effect, but it can modify the effect of the period. The model includes the period term and the period’s interaction with the characteristic:

the period coefficient is the log odds ratio for after against before in the reference category;
each interaction coefficient is how much larger or smaller that log odds ratio is in another category.

Two quantities follow.
The effect within each category. The log odds ratio in a non-reference category is the period coefficient plus that category’s interaction coefficient. Its standard error comes from the variances of the two coefficients and their covariance: Var(β₁ + β₂) = Var(β₁) + Var(β₂) + 2 Cov(β₁, β₂). Stata’s lincom 1.period + 1.period#2.group computes this. Fitting the model separately within each category gives the same odds ratio, which makes a useful check.
Whether the effect differs at all. A joint test that every interaction coefficient is zero: a Wald test, with as many degrees of freedom as there are interaction coefficients. This is Stata’s testparm. Its P value answers “is the change the same in every category?”, not “did this category change?”. A characteristic can have one category whose change is clearly significant and another whose change is not, while the interaction test shows no evidence that the changes differ; the categories’ own P values partly reflect how many people are in each.
When two characteristics are correlated, say age and years since diagnosis, an interaction with one may stand in for the other. Putting both interactions in one model shows whether each remains once the other is allowed for.

title: Methodological background
section: Comparing the change in two periods
text:
Comparing the change in two periods
Suppose the same people were measured before and after an event in two different eras, and the question is whether the change was larger in the later era. Stacking all four observations per person, with one stratum per person, the model has:

a period term: the change around the event in the reference era;
an era term: the difference between the two eras’ “before” measurements, within a person;
their interaction: how much larger the change around the event was in the other era, on the log-odds scale. Its exponent is a ratio of odds ratios.

This is a difference-in-differences on the log-odds scale, done within people. People measured in only one era still contribute: their pair informs the change around that era’s event, which for the later era is the period term plus the interaction. They cannot separate those two terms on their own, but pooled with people measured in both eras they shift the estimated interaction and its precision. Whether to keep them is a design choice: keeping them uses more data for one of the two changes, while restricting to people measured in both eras compares like with like.
Interacting every one of these terms with a characteristic (a three-way interaction) asks whether any part of the pattern differs between groups. With small groups such models often fail to converge: some combination of era, period and category has no discordant pairs, and its coefficient runs off to infinity.

title: Methodological background
Methodological background
text:
Missing outcomes
When an outcome can be missing, for example a laboratory result that was never drawn, two simple choices give different answers:

Missing as failure: count a missing result as the bad outcome. Every person stays in the analysis, but if missing results become less common after the event (because people re-entered care and were tested), the change is partly a change in testing.
Missing as missing: drop the observation. In a paired analysis a person missing one of the two measurements then drops out altogether, and the comparison rests on those tested both times.

Reporting both shows how much the answer depends on the choice.

McNemar’s test
For engagement and retention, McNemar’s test on each patient’s pair of values (Methodological background), with the proportions before and after. It uses the wide data, one row per patient, because a pair is one row there. The original code ran it to confirm that the conditional logistic regression in the next script gives the same answer; for matched pairs the model’s score test is McNemar’s chi-squared test, while the model’s reported Wald P value tests the same hypothesis and is close but not identical. If no pair is discordant there is nothing to test: the statistics are missing and n_discordant is 0, and the script carries on.

Decision pending: the original code did not run McNemar’s test for viral suppression, though the article’s Methods describe it for all three outcomes. Whether to add it is decision issue #3.

Two race variables, as in the original code: an African American indicator, from race code 2, and the four race groups, from the study sheet’s code list (Setup). The indicator is a factor with “No” first, so “No” is the reference, as Stata’s i.AfricanAmerican makes 0 the base. rush_era is 1 for every row.
The printed table has one row per race code, with the recorded text it stands for, its group, and the number of rows. This is what the original code’s tab NewRace Race showed, and it is how an authorized analyst checks that each code is grouped as intended.


Click to show/hide R Code
# The original code's AfricanAmerican indicator and four race groups, from
# encode()'s race codes in the study sheet (R/setup.R). Stata's
# "generate AfricanAmerican=(Race==2)" is 0, not missing, when race is
# missing, so coalesce() makes a missing race "No" here too; the race
# groups stay missing. The table that
# follows shows which recorded value each code stands for, so an
# authorized analyst can check the grouping, as the original code's
# "tab NewRace Race" did.
study_long <- study_long |>
  mutate(
    african_american = factor(
      if_else(coalesce(race_code == african_american_code, FALSE), "Yes", "No"),
      levels = c("No", "Yes")
    ),
    race_group = group_race_codes(race_code, race_group_codes_study),
    rush_era = 1L
  )
study_long |>
  distinct(patient_number, race_code, race, race_group) |>
  count(race_code, race, race_group) |>
  print()

title: 2. Build long data
text:
Stack the eras
Both cohorts in one data frame, sorted by patient, era and period, as the original code’s append and sort. A patient with visits in both eras now has four rows.
Two things are done differently from the original code, and both are listed on Differences from the original code. The race codes are not comparable between the sheets, so only the race groups are used from here on, and race as recorded is kept as text. Sex and age group are stacked as their recorded text and then given the study cohort’s category order, so a value that is missing from one sheet cannot shift the meaning of the other sheet’s codes, as it could have when Stata appended the numbered versions.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Both eras together, sorted by patient, era and period, as the original
# code's append and sort. The two sheets' race codes are not comparable, so
# the stacked data use the race groups, never the codes. Sex and age group
# are stacked as their recorded text (factor levels), so a level missing
# from one sheet cannot shift the other's categories.
both_eras_long <- bind_rows(
  study_long |> mutate(race = as.character(race)),
  control_long |> mutate(race = as.character(race))
) |>
  mutate(
    gender = fct_relevel(factor(gender), levels(study_long$gender)),
    age_group = fct_relevel(factor(age_group), levels(study_long$age_group)),
    race_group = factor(race_group, levels = race_group_levels)
  ) |>
  arrange(patient_number, rush_era, post_visit)

Data files
The workbooks are found only through the RUSH_DATA_DIR setting, which an authorized analyst puts in their own .Renviron; the repository holds no path to them. The original code had a global, $DateOfAnalysis, holding the date in the file names, and set Stata’s working directory to a folder on the analyst’s computer. Here the date is a constant and the folder is the setting.

# that date, as in the Stata file's $DateOfAnalysis global.

text:
Categories
Years since diagnosis comes as text groups, and the original code turned them into numbered categories in this order, “5 or fewer” first, so that group is the reference. Viral load comes as the text “Suppressed” or “Not Suppressed”; anything else, including an empty cell, is missing.
Race needs the longest comment. The original code turned the recorded race text into numbers with Stata’s encode, which numbers distinct values alphabetically, and then grouped the numbers, not the text: in the study sheet codes 4 and 7 are White, 1, 5 and 6 are Asian, other or unknown. Because each sheet was encoded separately, and the control sheet has fewer distinct values, the same code means different things in the two sheets, so each sheet has its own list. The lists are copied from the original code. What text each number stands for is not documented outside the data, so it is still to be checked; 2. Build long data prints the table needed for the check.
Study design and methods explains why race is used in four groups.

Models the original code could not fit
Three models are commented out in the original code, each with a note that the fit failed: race as recorded with viral suppression (missing excluded), and, in the era comparison with every patient, the race groups with viral suppression (missing as failure) and with retention. A conditional logistic regression fails like this when some combination of categories has no patients whose outcome changed, so a coefficient has no finite estimate. The R version skips the same three, so it fits the same set of models; the lists are tables so a reader can see them at a glance.

title: 4. RUSH-era models
text: This script fits the conditional logistic regressions for the RUSH-era cohort: the effect of the visit on each outcome, whether it differs by each patient characteristic, and the multivariable models. Every model has one stratum per patient, so each patient is compared only with themself.

title: 4. RUSH-era models
text:
The effect of the visit
One model per outcome, with post_visit as the only term: the original code’s first four clogit commands. The odds ratio for post_visit compares the odds of the outcome after the visit with before it, within patients. With two records per patient it equals the number of patients who improved divided by the number who got worse, which the synthetic test checks (Methodological background).
For viral suppression with missing results excluded, a patient tested in only one window has a single record in their stratum and contributes nothing, so this model rests on patients tested both times.


Click to show/hide R Code
# The effect of the visit on each outcome (analysis-plan.md 8.3): one
# stratum per patient, so each patient is compared with themself before and
# after. The odds ratio for post_visit is the conditional odds ratio; for a
# before-and-after pair it rests only on the patients whose outcome changed,
# like McNemar's test.
visit_models <- list()
for (outcome in names(outcomes)) {
  visit_models[[outcome]] <- fit_conditional_logit(
    study_long, outcome, "post_visit"
  )
}
visit_effects <- list()
for (outcome in names(outcomes)) {
  visit_effects[[outcome]] <- tidy_odds_ratios(
    visit_models[[outcome]], confidence_level
  )
}
visit_effects <- bind_rows(visit_effects, .id = "outcome")

title: 4. RUSH-era models
text:
Subgroup models
For each characteristic and outcome, post_visit plus its interaction with the characteristic (analysis plan §8.4). The models are stored as subgroup_models[[characteristic]][[outcome]]. The one model the original code could not fit is skipped by looking it up in the table on Setup, so the list of skipped models lives in one place.
.data$outcome and .env$outcome tell filter() which outcome is the table’s column and which is the loop’s variable, which share a name.


Click to show/hide R Code
# For each characteristic and outcome (analysis-plan.md 8.4), a model with
# the visit and its interaction with the characteristic, Stata's
# "i.Intervention##i.<characteristic>". The characteristic's own main
# effect is not written: it does not change within a patient, so it cannot
# be estimated. Models the original code could not fit are skipped
# (R/setup.R).
subgroup_models <- list()
for (subgroup in names(subgroups_rush)) {
  for (outcome in names(outcomes)) {
    skipped <- skipped_rush_subgroup_models |>
      filter(.data$outcome == .env$outcome, .data$subgroup == .env$subgroup)
    if (nrow(skipped) > 0) {
      next
    }
    subgroup_models[[subgroup]][[outcome]] <- fit_conditional_logit(
      study_long,
      outcome,
      str_glue("post_visit + post_visit:{subgroup}")
    )
  }
}

title: 4. RUSH-era models
text:
Does the effect differ?
For each model, the joint Wald test that every interaction coefficient is zero: is the change around the visit the same in every category? This is the original code’s testparm, and the P value the article gives when it says the improvement did, or did not, differ by a characteristic. Methodological background explains why this is a different question from whether each category improved.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Does the visit's effect differ across the categories? A joint Wald test
# that every interaction coefficient is zero, as the original code's
# testparm. For a two-category characteristic it is the test of the single
# interaction coefficient.
subgroup_tests <- list()
for (subgroup in names(subgroup_models)) {
  for (outcome in names(subgroup_models[[subgroup]])) {
    model <- subgroup_models[[subgroup]][[outcome]]
    subgroup_tests[[subgroup]][[outcome]] <- wald_test(
      model,
      interaction_terms("post_visit", subgroup, model$xlevels[[subgroup]])
    )
  }
}

section: Years since diagnosis and age together
text:
Years since diagnosis and age together
Patients diagnosed long ago tend to be older, so a difference by years since diagnosis might be a difference by age, or the reverse. One model with both interactions, and a test and within-category odds ratios for each, shows whether each difference remains once the other is allowed for. Each characteristic’s odds ratios here are for its categories with the other at its reference category.

# Years since diagnosis and age group in one model, each interacting with
# the visit, to see whether the differences by years since diagnosis remain
# once age is allowed for (analysis-plan.md 8.4)
combined_models <- list()
combined_tests <- list()
combined_effects <- list()
for (outcome in names(outcomes)) {
  model <- fit_conditional_logit(
    study_long,
    outcome,
    "post_visit + post_visit:years_since_dx_group + post_visit:age_group"
  )
  combined_models[[outcome]] <- model
  for (subgroup in c("years_since_dx_group", "age_group")) {
    combined_tests[[outcome]][[subgroup]] <- wald_test(
      model,
      interaction_terms("post_visit", subgroup, model$xlevels[[subgroup]])
    )
    combined_effects[[outcome]][[subgroup]] <- effect_by_level(
      model, subgroup, confidence_level
    )
  }
}

title: 4. RUSH-era models
text:
Multivariable models
post_visit with its interactions with year, sex, age group and race, in one model, for three outcomes: once with the African American indicator and once with race as recorded (analysis plan §8.5). The original code did not fit them for viral suppression with missing results excluded. They are tabulated as odds ratios for every coefficient, as Stata printed them.


Click to show/hide R Code
# All characteristics together, each interacting with the visit
# (analysis-plan.md 8.5): once with the African American indicator and once
# with race as recorded. The original code fitted these for three outcomes,
# leaving out viral suppression with missing results excluded.
multivariable_outcomes <- c(
  "vl_suppressed_missing_fail", "engaged_in_care", "retained_in_care"
)
multivariable_terms <- c(
  african_american = str_c(
    "post_visit + post_visit:index_test_year + post_visit:gender + ",
    "post_visit:age_group + post_visit:african_american"
  ),
  race = str_c(
    "post_visit + post_visit:index_test_year + post_visit:gender + ",
    "post_visit:age_group + post_visit:race"
  )
)
multivariable_models <- list()
multivariable_effects <- list()
for (version in names(multivariable_terms)) {
  for (outcome in multivariable_outcomes) {
    model <- fit_conditional_logit(
      study_long, outcome, multivariable_terms[[version]]
    )
    multivariable_models[[version]][[outcome]] <- model
    multivariable_effects[[version]][[outcome]] <- tidy_odds_ratios(
      model, confidence_level
    )
  }
}

This repository

How this website was created
The site is built with Quarto from the analysis scripts themselves. Each code page imports the labelled sections of its script from R/ and shows them with an explanation; the site never runs the analysis, so it is built without the study data.
The repository was set up with the R Analysis Workflow plugin for AI coding assistants, written by Vagish Hemmige, following the layout of COVID-infection-control. An AI assistant (Claude) translated the Stata code to R and drafted the documentation under the rules in AGENTS.md: it works only with code, documentation and synthetic data, never with the study data, and every change is reviewed and approved by Vagish Hemmige before it is merged.
Four documents describe the project:

Analysis plan: what the analysis does, and why. The published methods, following STROBE and RECORD.
Architecture: how the code does it. The scripts, the order they run in, what each needs and produces, and how data flow between them.
AGENTS.md: how people and AI assistants work on the project.
Repository blueprint: the layout every project of this kind starts from.

The pages

Home: the study in brief, what the site does, and its status.
Clinical background: opt-out testing, the HIV care continuum, and the RUSH program.
Methodological background: paired binary data, McNemar’s test, conditional logistic regression, interactions, comparing two eras, fixed and random person effects, and Stata-to-R equivalents.
Study design and methods: what this study chose and why, in plain language.

Setup and Functions: packages, constants and helper functions.

2. Build long data: two rows per patient, viral load outcomes, race groups, and the stacked eras.

References


Flash, Charlene A, Siavash Pasalar, Vagish Hemmige, et al. 2015. “Benefits of a Routine Opt-Out HIV Testing and Linkage to Care Program for Previously Diagnosed Patients in Publicly Funded Emergency Departments in Houston, TX.” Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes 69 (Suppl 1): S8–15. https://doi.org/10.1097/QAI.0000000000000578.
Project documentsAGENTS.md Code

The project
This repository is a teaching resource built on a published retrospective cohort study: the Routine Universal Screening for HIV (RUSH) program of opt-out HIV testing with service linkage in the Ben Taub and Lyndon B. Johnson emergency departments of Harris Health System, Houston, and its effect on engagement in care, retention in care and viral suppression among patients already diagnosed with HIV, compared before and after an emergency department visit in 2009 to 2012, and against a pre-RUSH era (J Acquir Immune Defic Syndr 2015, doi:10.1097/QAI.0000000000000578). The original analysis was one Stata .do file of January 2015, kept in stata/ with only its local folder path removed. This version rebuilds it in R as labelled scripts and explains each step on a Quarto website. The code is shown, not run on the study data here: the data are not in the repository, and the site’s results, including its versions of the article’s tables, are the published article’s values, not outputs of this code.

analysis-plan.md is the source of truth for design. Code implements the plan; it does not redefine it. If code needs to depart from the plan, open a decision issue, or comment on the existing one, for the deciders. Once a decider has settled it (in the issue, or relayed there in their exact words), the plan change and the code can go in the same pull request, which closes the issue.
Deciders. Scientific decisions are made by Vagish Hemmige, in any area. Anyone may open or contribute to a decision issue; only a decider settles it (see “Working with agents”).
Departures from the original analysis. The original Stata code and the paper are the record of what was done. When the R code differs from the Stata code, or the Stata code from the paper, do not silently copy it or silently fix it: the site’s “Differences from the original code” page records every difference, and choices between the paper and the code go to a decision issue.
The original code is a record. stata/RUSH_analysis_2015-01-15.do is not edited, except to remove private information (a local path, a name that is not an author’s); each such change is listed in its header.
This is an analysis project, not an R package. Do not add DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, roxygen, or pkgdown infrastructure, or apply CRAN conventions.
Default branch: main, protected. Changes reach it only through pull requests.

For a source with no package: the loading script records where the file comes from, its date, and any processing. Verify its columns against what the paper describes; never infer a column’s meaning from its name. The outcome columns arrive already derived (0 or 1, or a viral load result as text): how they were derived from the medical record and CPCDMS visit data is described only by the article.

R scripts

Running the analysis. Only an authorized person runs R/main.R, from the project root, with the data folder set in .Renviron. It sources the other scripts in dependency order; ARCHITECTURE.md describes what each does.
One job per script. When you add a definitive script, source it from main.R at the right point and update ARCHITECTURE.md in the same pull request.
Header comment. Each script begins with what it does, which objects it needs from earlier scripts, and what it produces.
Constants and libraries live in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library(), re-source setup.R, or hard-code values. File and sheet names, expected columns, category orders, race code lists and the models the original code skipped are named constants there.
Helper functions go in R/functions.R. A function takes its inputs as arguments and does not read global objects.
No side effects outside the project. No setwd(), absolute paths, or writes outside the project. The data are located only through RUSH_DATA_DIR. The scripts write no files; results stay as objects in the session.
No results in the repository. No script, comment, commit message, issue, pull-request text or review report contains counts or values from the study data beyond what the published article reports. Numbers quoted from the article are public and may be cited, with their location in the article.

Synthetic data and tests

tests/synthetic/build_synthetic_data.R writes random workbooks with the expected sheets, columns and value formats; nothing in them comes from the study. tests/synthetic/run_pipeline.R runs R/main.R on them and checks the helpers against results known from theory (the conditional odds ratio of paired data, the within-category odds ratio, the Wald and McNemar statistics).
.github/workflows/test-pipeline.yml runs it on every pull request. Agents may run it too.
Synthetic values are invented labels where the real ones are unknown (for example “Race A”); they must never be presented as the study’s categories.

Chunk labels
Scripts are divided into labelled sections so Quarto pages can show the code without copying it:
## ---- <step-name>

Every logical step has a label. A label covers the code from its line to the next label.
Labels are kebab-case, describe the step, and are unique across all scripts; a duplicate silently picks up the wrong code.
Search the .qmd files before renaming or deleting a label.
Labels are comments and never change what the code does.

Quarto website
The site documents the code. It does not run the analysis.

_quarto.yml, index.qmd, 404.qmd and styles.css sit at the root; quarto/ has one page per definitive script, named after it. The custom-callout extension in _extensions/ provides the Rcode, Results and Pending callouts.
Each page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") in a hidden chunk and shows each labelled section with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what the section does and why. Pages link to the script on GitHub and to the scripts it depends on.

The original Stata code page is R code (it is code). The differences page is study design and methods. The published results page is results, and its notice says the numbers are quoted from the article, not produced by this code.
Published tables are shown as tables rebuilt from the values the article prints: the values are typed into quarto/published/table_1.csv and tables_2_to_4.csv, exactly as printed, and formatted by the same functions R/tables.R uses on the data. Each table cites its place in the article and says it is not output of this code. Values that look inconsistent are kept as printed and noted, never corrected. The journal’s own typeset tables and Figure 1 are not copied; they need the publisher’s permission (RightsLink), after which the page notice states it.
Provisional content. quarto/_pending.lua highlights in yellow every paragraph that starts with Decision pending:, every paragraph of the plan’s page that contains the plan’s Open: marker, and any [text]{.pending}, and adds a ⏳ Pending callout to pages that have a mark. Mark only what an open decision could change, link its decision issue, and remove the mark when the decision is settled.
Never evaluate analysis code in the site. The only chunks that run are the hidden read_chunk() imports, the Architecture page’s reader of ARCHITECTURE.md, the readers of the .do file (quarto/_stata_sections.R, used by the original-code page and the folded “Original Stata code” boxes on the script pages), which read that file as text, and the published-results page’s chunks, which read the two published-values CSVs and format them with the table functions in R/functions.R. None reads study data or fits a model.
The site renders to docs/, which is not committed. .github/workflows/publish.yml renders it on every pull request as a check and, on each push to main, publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. When you add a script, add its page and sidebar entry in the same pull request.
Prose must match the code. If a change alters what a section does, update its explanation in the same pull request.

Outputs

R/tables.R writes HTML copies of Tables 1 to 4 to tables/, which is gitignored: tables made from the study data are not published. figures/ is gitignored too, in case a figure is added.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md; edit the .Rmd and re-knit.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)

Never commit data, extracts, saved objects, Stata logs, or outputs made from the study data. Check .gitignore before adding a new output type.
AI agents never read the study data. Anything an agent opens, prints, or summarizes is sent to the model provider. Agents do not open the data files, the 2015 Stata log, or outputs made from them. Agents write and review code and run it on synthetic data; only an authorized person runs it on the study data.
Credentials. Never commit keys, tokens, or .Renviron.

Coding conventions

Pre and post. post_visit is 0 for the period before the index visit and 1 for the period after it, whatever the outcome’s window (analysis-plan.md section 7); rush_era is 1 for the RUSH-era visit and 0 for the pre-RUSH visit.
Conditional logistic regression is survival::clogit() through fit_conditional_logit(), with one stratum per patient and the exact conditional likelihood. In the RUSH-era models a characteristic, which cannot change within a patient there, enters only through its interactions with post_visit. The era models use the full factorial (post_visit * rush_era * characteristic), because a characteristic taken from each era’s sheet can differ between a patient’s visits.
Category order and reference levels match the original code: text categories are numbered as Stata’s encode numbered them (encode_like_stata()), so the first level is Stata’s base level. Do not reorder levels in the models without a decision issue.
Race codes. The two workbook sheets number race values separately. Race groups are made from each sheet’s own codes, and only the groups, never the codes, are used once the eras are stacked.
Reported quantities (odds ratios within a category, joint interaction tests) come from the named functions in R/functions.R, which are checked on synthetic data.
Package APIs: read the help page and NEWS for the installed version before calling a package; don’t write calls from memory.
Style: readable tidyverse code, following the tidyverse style guide: dplyr pipelines (|>), one step per line; case_when() rather than nested ifelse(); models, rows and columns selected by name, never by position; repeated fits as for-loops over names into named lists. Style changes go in their own commits.

Checks for any change

Plan: does the change implement the plan as written, and does it leave every open decision open?
Departures: does every difference from the original Stata code appear on the differences page, and is each either a correction of an error or linked to a decision issue?
Models: is each model fitted within patient strata; does every interaction test find its coefficients (Rscript tests/synthetic/run_pipeline.R passes)?
Reported numbers: does site prose say what the code computes, and is every number quoted from the article cited to its place there?
Structure: is ARCHITECTURE.md current; are chunk labels unique and found by their pages; does every definitive script have a page and a sidebar entry with its kind’s icon; does any site chunk run analysis code?
Disclosure: search changed files, commit messages and pull-request text for counts or values from the study data that the article does not report.

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent decides how much it may do, and may give it stricter rules of their own; those take precedence. By default an agent may edit code and documentation, run the synthetic tests, render the site, and commit to a branch and open a pull request.
Decisions. Anyone, including an agent, may add options and evidence to a decision issue. A decider states the choice in the issue. Agents implement decisions; they never choose among options on their own, in the issue, the plan, or the code.
Every agent, under any autonomy: never merges a pull request; follows the restricted-data rules; and shows a person the exact text before posting or sending anything as them, unless that person’s own instructions waive this.
Pull requests opened by an agent are focused. Each says which plan section or issue it addresses and what was checked, and how.
References: cite the source documentation and literature used, in references.bib.
Project documentsRepository blueprint Code

Analytical scripts

R/main.R sources definitive scripts in dependency order.
Typical workflow: setup → cohort construction → processing → modeling → outputs.
Study-specific scripts may be grouped into subdirectories by analytical stage.
R/tables.R and R/figures.R may generate outputs directly or orchestrate specialized scripts.

Documentation

Document definitive analytical scripts with explanatory Quarto pages; exploratory scripts need not have pages.
Use Cryptococcus-cost-analysis as an example for Quarto supporting files, chunk imports, callouts, and formatting—not scientific methods.
Quarto source and rendered output locations may vary by project.

Outputs and version control

Track approved, nonrestricted outputs when useful for publication; otherwise retain them locally and exclude them from Git.
.gitignore: Exclude restricted data, credentials, caches, temporary files, and generated outputs unless intentionally tracked (e.g., .Rproj.user/, .Rhistory, .RData, .httr-oauth, .quarto/, cache/, figures/, tables/, *.quarto_ipynb); verify exclusions cover actual output paths without hiding necessary source or reference files.

text: This script builds the article’s four tables from the data with gtsummary: Table 1, the two cohorts’ characteristics, and Tables 2 to 4, each outcome before and after the visit within every subgroup. The Stata code made none of them. On this site the tables are shown filled with the article’s printed values (Published results), laid out by the same functions; the script itself writes HTML copies to tables/, which is never committed.

title: Tables
text:
One row per patient
The long data have two rows per patient; a table of patients needs one. Selecting the patient number and the characteristics, which are the same in both of a patient’s rows, and keeping distinct rows gives one row per patient in each cohort.
The control sheet has no years since diagnosis. The controls are the same patients as the study cohort, with the same patient numbers, so their group is joined from the study cohort. The years workbook holds years from diagnosis to the RUSH-era index visit, so that is the value the controls’ column shows.


Click to show/hide R Code
# One row per patient in each cohort, with the characteristics the tables
# use. They are the same in a patient's before and after rows.
study_patients <- study_long |>
  select(patient_number, any_of(names(table_characteristics))) |>
  distinct()
# The controls are the same patients as the study cohort, with the same
# patient numbers, so their years since diagnosis come from the years
# workbook through the study cohort. That workbook holds years from
# diagnosis to the RUSH-era index visit, so this is the value used.
control_patients <- control_long |>
  select(patient_number, any_of(names(table_characteristics))) |>
  distinct() |>
  left_join(
    study_patients |> select(patient_number, years_since_dx_group),
    by = "patient_number",
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  )

Most people who test positive in a busy emergency department’s routine HIV testing program already know they have HIV. In Houston’s Routine Universal Screening for HIV (RUSH) program, about three in four positives were previously diagnosed. Many of them are out of care, so the visit is a chance to bring them back. Flash and colleagues asked whether it does: among 2,068 previously diagnosed patients tested in the Ben Taub and Lyndon B. Johnson emergency departments between 2009 and 2012, they compared each patient’s engagement in care, retention in care and viral suppression in the months before the visit with the same outcomes in the months after it, and compared that change with the change around an earlier visit by 672 of the same patients, before RUSH and its service linkage workers existed (Flash et al. 2015).
All three outcomes improved after the visit: engagement from 41.3% to 58.8%, retention from 32.6% to 47.1%, and viral suppression from 22.8% to 34.0%, each with P < 0.001 (abstract), and each improvement was larger than around the pre-RUSH visit (Flash et al. 2015). Clinical background explains the program and why previously diagnosed patients matter.

title: RUSH: re-linkage to HIV care after routine testing in the emergency department
text:
What this site does
This site is a teaching resource. It uses the published study to show how a paired before-and-after analysis is built: McNemar’s test, conditional logistic regression with one stratum per patient, interactions to see whether an effect differs between groups, and a comparison of two eras. The original analysis was one Stata .do file of January 2015. Here it is rebuilt in R as labelled scripts, each page explaining what a section of the code does and why, and the original Stata code is shown alongside for comparison.
The code is shown, not run. The de-identified patient data are Harris Health System data and are not in this repository, so no result on this site comes from running the code. The study’s results are those published in the article, quoted with their place there on Published results. The R code has been run only on synthetic data, to check that it runs and that its helper functions give the answers known from theory.

section: Number categories as Stata’s encode did
text:
Number categories as Stata’s encode did
Stata’s encode turns text into numbered categories in alphabetical order, treating empty text as missing; the first becomes the base level in models. To fit the same models with the same reference categories, R needs factors whose levels are in the same order. sort(method = "radix") sorts in byte order, as Stata does, regardless of the computer’s language settings; R’s ordinary sort can place capitals and accented letters differently. The codes are then as.integer() of the factor.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Stata's encode turns a text variable into numbered categories, numbering
# the distinct values in alphabetical (byte) order, with empty text as
# missing. This returns a factor with its levels in that order, so the
# reference level and the codes match the original code. The codes are
# as.integer() of the factor.
encode_like_stata <- function(x) {
  x <- na_if(x, "")
  value_order <- sort(unique(x[!is.na(x)]), method = "radix")
  factor(x, levels = value_order)
}

title: Functions
text:
Clean a cohort
What both workbook sheets need before they can be reshaped: drop the unused _Place columns; give the outcome columns names ending in _0 (before the visit) and _1 (after it), as the original code renamed them for Stata’s reshape; number race, sex and age group as encode did, keeping race’s numeric code for the race groups; and make the year of the visit a category, as Stata’s i.IndexTestYear treats it, with 2009 as the reference. The year is renamed only where present, because the control sheet need not have it.


Click to show/hide R Code
# The cleaning both cohorts share: drop the unused place columns, number the
# text categories as Stata's encode did, keep each race value's code for
# the race groups (R/02_build_long_data.R), and give the outcome columns
# names ending in _0 (before the visit) and _1 (after it), as the original
# code's renames did before reshaping.
clean_cohort <- function(cohort_raw, place_columns) {
  cohort_raw |>
    select(-all_of(place_columns)) |>
    rename(
      patient_number = PatientNumber,
      engaged_in_care_0 = EngageInCare_Before,
      engaged_in_care_1 = EngagedInCare_After,
      retained_in_care_0 = RetainedInCare_Before,
      retained_in_care_1 = RetainedInCare_After,
      vl_0 = VL_Before,
      vl_1 = VL_After
    ) |>
    # The original code never reads the year in the control sheet, so it
    # is renamed only where present
    rename(any_of(c(index_test_year = "IndexTestYear"))) |>
    mutate(
      race = encode_like_stata(Race),
      race_code = as.integer(race),
      gender = encode_like_stata(Gender),
      age_group = encode_like_stata(AgeGroup),
      # Stata's i.IndexTestYear treats each year as a category, with the
      # earliest as the reference
      across(any_of("index_test_year"), factor)
    ) |>
    select(-Race, -Gender, -AgeGroup)
}

Two binary versions of the viral load result (analysis plan §7): vl_suppressed is missing when the result is, and vl_suppressed_missing_fail counts a missing result as not suppressed. coalesce() replaces the missing values with 0, as the original code’s replace … if … == . did.

# Two binary viral load outcomes (analysis-plan.md 7.3): vl_suppressed keeps
# a missing result missing; vl_suppressed_missing_fail counts it as not
# suppressed. A value other than the two recorded results is also missing,
# as in the original code.
add_viral_load_outcomes <- function(cohort_long, suppressed, not_suppressed) {
  cohort_long |>
    mutate(
      vl_suppressed = case_when(
        vl == suppressed ~ 1L,
        vl == not_suppressed ~ 0L,
        .default = NA_integer_
      ),
      vl_suppressed_missing_fail = coalesce(vl_suppressed, 0L)
    )
}

title: Functions
text:
McNemar’s test
The paired test of Methodological background. It returns the four kinds of pair, the proportions before and after, the uncorrected chi-squared statistic and its P value, and the exact P value from a binomial test on the discordant pairs, which is what Stata’s mcc reports. Writing the statistic out makes it visible that only the discordant pairs matter. With no discordant pairs, or no complete pairs, there is no test; the function returns missing statistics with n_discordant and n_pairs, which say which case it is, instead of stopping the whole pipeline.


Click to show/hide R Code
# McNemar's test for one binary outcome measured before and after the visit
# on the same patients, as Stata's mcc reports it: the four paired counts,
# the uncorrected chi-squared test, and the exact test (a binomial test on
# the discordant pairs). Patients missing either value are left out. With
# no complete pairs, or no discordant pairs, there is no test: the
# statistics are missing and n_pairs and n_discordant say why, so the
# pipeline carries on to the other outcomes.
paired_mcnemar <- function(cohort_wide, before, after) {
  pairs <- cohort_wide |>
    filter(!is.na(.data[[before]]), !is.na(.data[[after]]))
  counts <- pairs |>
    count(before = .data[[before]], after = .data[[after]])
  n_after_only <- sum(pairs[[before]] == 0 & pairs[[after]] == 1)
  n_before_only <- sum(pairs[[before]] == 1 & pairs[[after]] == 0)
  n_discordant <- n_after_only + n_before_only
  chi_squared <- NA_real_
  p_value <- NA_real_
  p_value_exact <- NA_real_
  odds_ratio <- NA_real_
  conf_low <- NA_real_
  conf_high <- NA_real_
  if (n_discordant > 0) {
    chi_squared <- (n_after_only - n_before_only)^2 / n_discordant
    p_value <- pchisq(chi_squared, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
    exact <- binom.test(n_after_only, n_discordant)
    p_value_exact <- exact$p.value
    # The matched-pairs odds ratio, after-only over before-only pairs, with
    # the exact interval mcc reports: the binomial interval for the share of
    # discordant pairs that improved, p, turned into odds p / (1 - p). It is
    # infinite when no pair got worse, as the article's Table 4 footnotes.
    odds_ratio <- n_after_only / n_before_only
    conf_low <- exact$conf.int[1] / (1 - exact$conf.int[1])
    conf_high <- exact$conf.int[2] / (1 - exact$conf.int[2])
  }
  list(
    counts = counts,
    n_pairs = nrow(pairs),
    n_discordant = n_discordant,
    proportion_before = if (nrow(pairs) > 0) mean(pairs[[before]]) else NA_real_,
    proportion_after = if (nrow(pairs) > 0) mean(pairs[[after]]) else NA_real_,
    n_before = sum(pairs[[before]]),
    n_after = sum(pairs[[after]]),
    odds_ratio = odds_ratio,
    conf_low = conf_low,
    conf_high = conf_high,
    chi_squared = chi_squared,
    p_value = p_value,
    p_value_exact = p_value_exact
  )
}

text:
Combine coefficients
The odds ratio, confidence interval and P value for a sum of coefficients, which is what Stata’s lincom …, or reports. The variance of a sum is the sum of every variance and covariance among its terms, which is the sum of every cell of the covariance matrix restricted to those terms; that is the one line of matrix algebra. If a coefficient could not be estimated, it returns missing values rather than an answer from part of the sum.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Odds ratio, confidence interval and Wald P value for a sum of
# coefficients, as Stata's "lincom ..., or" reports it. Base R matrix algebra
# is needed for the variance of a sum: it is the sum of the variances and
# covariances of the coefficients in the sum.
combine_coefficients <- function(model, terms, level = 0.95) {
  estimates <- model_coefficients(model)$estimates
  if (!all(terms %in% names(estimates)) || anyNA(estimates[terms])) {
    return(tibble(
      log_odds_ratio = NA_real_, std_error = NA_real_,
      odds_ratio = NA_real_, conf_low = NA_real_, conf_high = NA_real_,
      p_value = NA_real_
    ))
  }
  covariance <- model_coefficients(model)$covariance[terms, terms, drop = FALSE]
  log_odds_ratio <- sum(estimates[terms])
  std_error <- sqrt(sum(covariance))
  z <- qnorm(1 - (1 - level) / 2)
  tibble(
    log_odds_ratio = log_odds_ratio,
    std_error = std_error,
    odds_ratio = exp(log_odds_ratio),
    conf_low = exp(log_odds_ratio - z * std_error),
    conf_high = exp(log_odds_ratio + z * std_error),
    p_value = 2 * pnorm(-abs(log_odds_ratio / std_error))
  )
}

text:
Joint Wald test
The test that a set of coefficients are all zero, b' V⁻¹ b compared with a chi-squared distribution with as many degrees of freedom as coefficients: Stata’s testparm. A coefficient that could not be estimated is left out, as Stata leaves it out. If none can be estimated the test is missing, with zero degrees of freedom; the synthetic test fails if that happens to any interaction test, which would also catch a misspelled coefficient name.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Joint Wald test that a set of coefficients are all zero, as Stata's
# testparm reports it. Coefficients R could not estimate (NA, as when a
# level has no information) are left out, as Stata omits them; the degrees
# of freedom are the number tested.
wald_test <- function(model, terms) {
  estimates <- model_coefficients(model)$estimates
  terms <- terms[terms %in% names(estimates) & !is.na(estimates[terms])]
  if (length(terms) == 0) {
    return(tibble(chi_squared = NA_real_, df = 0L, p_value = NA_real_))
  }
  # Base R matrix algebra: the Wald statistic b' V^-1 b
  b <- estimates[terms]
  covariance <- model_coefficients(model)$covariance[terms, terms, drop = FALSE]
  chi_squared <- as.numeric(t(b) %*% solve(covariance) %*% b)
  tibble(
    chi_squared = chi_squared,
    df = length(terms),
    p_value = pchisq(chi_squared, df = length(terms), lower.tail = FALSE)
  )
}

Odds ratio table
Every coefficient of a model as an odds ratio with its confidence interval and P value, the table Stata prints with the or option. It uses combine_coefficients() with one term at a time, so its intervals and P values are computed exactly as the within-category ones are.

# Every coefficient as an odds ratio with a Wald confidence interval and P
# value, as Stata's "or" option shows them. Works for clogit() and glmer()
# models; for glmer() these are the fixed effects.
tidy_odds_ratios <- function(model, level = 0.95) {
  estimates <- model_coefficients(model)$estimates
  results <- list()
  for (term in names(estimates)) {
    results[[term]] <- combine_coefficients(model, term, level)
  }
  bind_rows(results, .id = "term")
}

title: Functions
section: Format a row of Tables 2 to 4
text:
Format a row of Tables 2 to 4
Turns the counts and the model’s odds ratio for the visit into the text cells of a row: the odds ratio with its Wald interval and the Wald P value, as the article prints them. gtsummary’s style_percent(), style_ratio() and style_pvalue() do the rounding. When no patient got worse the odds ratio is infinite: the model can only return a very large number with no usable interval, so the row prints “∞” and “-”, as the article’s Table 4 does. Whether that applies is read from the counts, not from the model. With no discordant pairs, or no fitted model, the cells are empty.


Click to show/hide R Code
# For Tables 2 to 4: one row of text, the columns format_outcome_table()
# expects, from count_pairs() and the odds ratio for the visit from the
# conditional logistic regression (one row of effect_by_level() or
# tidy_odds_ratios()). The interval and P value are the model's Wald ones,
# as the article prints them (decision in issue #5).
# A category in which no patient got worse has an infinite odds ratio: the
# model's estimate there is only a very large number with no usable
# interval or P value, so the row prints "∞" and "-", as the article's
# Table 4 does. No patient got better: "0" and "-". No discordant pairs, or
# no estimate (a model not fitted): the cells are empty.
format_change <- function(counts, effect) {
  has_estimate <- nrow(effect) == 1 && !is.na(effect$odds_ratio)
  odds_ratio_text <- ""
  p_value_text <- ""
  if (counts$n_worse > 0 && counts$n_better > 0 && has_estimate) {
    odds_ratio_text <- as.character(str_glue(
      "{style_ratio(effect$odds_ratio)} ",
      "({style_ratio(effect$conf_low)}–{style_ratio(effect$conf_high)})"
    ))
    p_value_text <- coalesce(style_pvalue(effect$p_value, digits = 3), "")
  } else if (counts$n_worse == 0 && counts$n_better > 0) {
    odds_ratio_text <- "∞"
    p_value_text <- "-"
  } else if (counts$n_better == 0 && counts$n_worse > 0) {
    odds_ratio_text <- "0"
    p_value_text <- "-"
  }
  tibble(
    n = as.character(counts$n_pairs),
    before_n = as.character(counts$n_before),
    before_pct = style_percent(counts$n_before / counts$n_pairs, suffix = "%"),
    after_n = as.character(counts$n_after),
    after_pct = style_percent(counts$n_after / counts$n_pairs, suffix = "%"),
    odds_ratio = odds_ratio_text,
    p_value = p_value_text
  )
}

This page explains, in plain language and without code, what this study chose and why. The general background it relies on is on Methodological background. The formal specification is the analysis plan; each section below ends by linking the part of the plan that governs it. Three kinds of note mark where the description stands:

title: Study design and methods
section: The question and the design in brief
text:
The question and the design in brief
Does an HIV test in an emergency department with routine testing and service linkage help a person who already knows they have HIV get back into care? The study answers it by comparing each patient with themself: their engagement, retention and viral suppression in the months before an emergency department visit against the same outcomes in the months after it. A second comparison, around an earlier visit by some of the same patients before the program existed, asks whether the change around a RUSH-era visit is larger than the change around any emergency department visit (Flash et al. 2015).
The before-and-after comparison within patients removes every stable difference between patients: sex, race, how long they have had HIV, and everything unmeasured that stays the same across the two windows. It does not remove what changes over time for everyone, such as treatment guidelines; the comparison with the pre-RUSH era addresses part of that.
Specified in: §1 Objective, §2 Design.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Who is in the study
The RUSH-era cohort is every previously diagnosed patient who tested positive in either emergency department between 2009 and 2012, at a visit at least a year after their original diagnosis, taking the first such visit per patient: 2,068 patients (Flash et al. 2015). The one-year rule keeps out people diagnosed so recently that they could not yet have been engaged, retained or suppressed in the “before” window, whose improvement would reflect the natural course of a new diagnosis rather than the visit.
The cohort was built before the analysis, from laboratory, surveillance, medical record and Ryan White visit data. The scripts here start from the de-identified workbooks, one row per patient, and apply no further exclusion.
Specified in: §3 Data source, §4 Study population.

title: Study design and methods
section: The windows before and after the visit
text:
The windows before and after the visit
Each outcome has its own window, the same length before and after the visit (Flash et al. 2015):

Engagement: 6 months. The authors chose 6 rather than 3 months because 3 months seemed too short a window for the period before the visit.
Retention: 12 months, with two visits at least 3 months apart.
Viral suppression: 12 months, shifted by 10 days. A viral load drawn in the days after the visit reflects treatment before it, so it belongs to the “before” window; the “after” window starts on day 11.

Visits count if they are in the Harris Health record or in the Houston area’s Ryan White visit database. Viral loads are only seen if drawn at Harris Health.
Specified in: §7 Outcomes.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Missing viral loads
About four in ten patients had no Harris Health viral load in a given window (the article reports results for 59% before and 56% after the visit, Results). The primary analysis counts a missing viral load as not suppressed; the secondary analysis leaves it missing, so only patients with a result in both windows inform that comparison. Counting missing as failure biases suppression downward in both windows; its effect on the change depends on whether testing itself became more common after the visit (see Methodological background).
Specified in: §7 Outcomes, §9 Sensitivity analyses.

title: Study design and methods
text:
The overall change
For each outcome, the proportion before and after the visit, compared with McNemar’s test, and the conditional odds ratio for after against before from a conditional logistic regression with one stratum per patient. For matched pairs the odds ratio is the ratio of patients who improved to patients who got worse, and the model’s score test is McNemar’s chi-squared test. The P value the code reports from the model is a Wald P value, which tests the same hypothesis but need not equal McNemar’s (in the example on Methodological background, 7.7 against 9.0 on one degree of freedom).
Specified in: §8.2 Overall change, §8.3 Conditional logistic regression.

Decision pending: the original code ran McNemar’s test for engagement and retention but not for viral suppression, while the article’s Methods describe it for all three. Whether the R version adds it for viral suppression is decision issue #3.

title: Study design and methods
section: Did the change differ between groups?
text:
Did the change differ between groups?
For sex, race and ethnicity, age group, year of the visit and years since diagnosis, the conditional model includes the interaction of the period with the characteristic. For each, the code reports the joint test that the change is the same in every category, and the odds ratio for the visit within each category. Race and ethnicity is used in four groups (Black, Hispanic, White and other), as the article reports it; the original code also tried race as recorded and an African American indicator. Age and years since diagnosis are correlated, so the original code also put both in one model.
The reference category for each is the first in the original code’s order, which is why the R code numbers categories the way Stata’s encode did.
Specified in: §8.4 Differences by patient characteristics, §8.5 Multivariable models.
Current code: the four race groups are made from Stata’s numeric codes for the recorded race values, as in the original code, because the recorded values themselves are not documented outside the data. Which value each code stands for is still to be checked against the data by an authorized analyst (issue #4); the code prints the table needed for that check.

title: Study design and methods
section: Comparing the RUSH era with the era before it
text:
Comparing the RUSH era with the era before it
672 of the patients had a qualifying emergency department visit in the four years before RUSH (the article’s example is 2004 to 2007), at least a year after diagnosis, with follow-up ending before the RUSH era; for each, the visit nearest their RUSH-era visit was used (Flash et al. 2015). Before RUSH there was no routine testing and no service linkage worker; referral was a phone number. Stacking both eras, each patient has up to four records, and the conditional model’s interaction of period and era asks whether the change around the RUSH-era visit was larger.
Using the same patients in both eras controls for who they are. It does not control for what changed between the eras for everyone: treatment guidelines, newer antiretrovirals, attention to retention, and the patients’ own longer time since diagnosis.
Specified in: §6 Comparator, §8.6 Comparison with the pre-RUSH era.

Decision pending: the original code fitted the era comparison twice, once with every patient (2,068; those with a RUSH-era visit only inform the RUSH-era change, and through it the era comparison, but cannot separate its parts) and once with only the patients who had a visit in both eras. The article does not say which produced its P values. This is decision issue #2.

title: Study design and methods
text:
Random-intercept models
For comparison, the original code also fitted the era model with a random intercept per patient instead of strata. It uses differences between patients too, and so rests on a stronger assumption (see Methodological background). It is a sensitivity analysis; the article reports the conditional model.
Specified in: §8.6, §9 Sensitivity analyses.

title: Differences from the original code
text:
Differences in what is reported

Within-category odds ratios and interaction tests for every characteristic. The original code ran testparm and lincom for most characteristics, but for sex only lincom (with one interaction term, that term’s own P value is the test), and for race as recorded neither. The R version computes both for every characteristic. This only adds output.
Multivariable models are tabulated as odds ratios for every coefficient, as Stata’s or option showed them.
Printed checks. R’s quantile() and Stata’s summarize, detail define percentiles slightly differently; R’s count() shows a row for missing values where Stata’s tab without missing hides it. The random-intercept tables do not show xtlogit’s intercept variance or its test that the variance is zero. None of these affects an estimate.
Unused variables are not made. The original code created HIV_tested_During_Visit (always 1) and encoded IndexTest_Place before dropping it; neither was used in any analysis.

title: Differences from the original code
section: Differences that could change a number
text:
Differences that could change a number

Sex and age group in the stacked eras. The original code encoded each sheet separately and then appended them, so the stacked data carried the study sheet’s numeric codes for sex and age group, with its labels. If the two sheets had the same set of recorded values, the codes agree and the results are the same. If a value was absent from one sheet, the codes after it would shift and a category would be mislabelled. The R version stacks the recorded text instead, so this cannot happen. Whether the sheets’ value sets match is part of the first run on the study data.
An omitted coefficient in a within-category odds ratio. If an interaction coefficient cannot be estimated, effect_by_level() reports that category’s odds ratio as missing. Stata’s lincom treats an omitted coefficient as zero and reports the reference category’s odds ratio for it. R’s answer is the honest one; it changes only categories for which Stata’s number was not an estimate.
Patients with no informative pairs. Like Stata, the R version fits each model to the patients whose outcome changed, and picks the reference category among the categories that still have such patients. A category with none is listed as not estimable. Stata drops the same patients; how its lincom output labels a category left with none has not been checked. Without this step the R version could have labelled one category’s odds ratio with another’s name.
Repeated patient numbers stop the import, as Stata’s merge 1:1 and reshape would have; the R join and reshape alone would not have.
McNemar’s test with no discordant pairs returns missing statistics instead of an error, so the other outcomes still run.
Excel column types. read_excel() is told to guess each column’s type from every row, as Stata’s import excel types the whole column. With R’s default of 1,000 rows, a viral load column empty in its first rows could have lost its later values.
Random-intercept models. Stata’s xtlogit and R’s glmer() both integrate over the random intercept by adaptive Gauss–Hermite quadrature with 12 points, but with different optimizers. Their estimates should agree closely, not exactly.

title: Differences from the original code
section: Kept as in the original, and still to check
text:
Kept as in the original, and still to check
These are not changed, because changing them would depart from the published analysis; each is recorded so it can be checked.

Race groups from numeric codes. The original code built the four race groups, and the African American indicator, from encode’s numeric codes, with a different list of codes for each sheet, because each sheet’s values were numbered separately. The R version does the same, with the code lists in R/setup.R, and prints the table of code, recorded value and group so it can be checked (issue #4).
The African American indicator when race is missing. Stata’s generate AfricanAmerican=(Race==2) is 0 for a patient with no recorded race, so those patients count as not African American in the African American models and the first set of multivariable models, while the race-group and race models leave them out. The R version reproduces this. It means the two multivariable versions can rest on slightly different samples.
Unmatched patients in the merge. The original code merged the years-since-diagnosis workbook one to one and kept every row, printing how many matched. A patient in only one file stays in the data with the other file’s columns missing. The R version does the same and prints the same counts.


The era-comparison sample
The original code fitted the era comparison twice, with every patient and with only the patients who had a visit in both eras. The R version fits both.

Decision pending: which of the two samples produced the P values the article reports (decision issue #2).



McNemar’s test for viral suppression
The original code ran McNemar’s test for engagement and retention only. The R version does the same.

Decision pending: whether to add it for viral suppression, as the article’s Methods describe (decision issue #3).

title: Differences from the original code
text:
Added: the article’s tables
The Stata code makes none of the article’s four tables. R/tables.R builds them with gtsummary, in the article’s layout, so the code shows how each was made:

Table 1 counts each cohort’s patients by sex, race group, visit year (paired by position across eras), age group and years since diagnosis. The control sheet holds no years since diagnosis; the controls are the same patients, so their groups are taken from the years workbook by patient number. That workbook gives years to the RUSH-era index visit, so the controls’ column uses that value. The Stata code never uses years since diagnosis for the controls; the article’s control column, which may be years to the pre-RUSH visit, probably came from the SPSS work the article mentions, so the two columns need not match.
Tables 2 to 4 show, for each subgroup, the patients with both values, the number with the outcome before and after, the odds ratio for the visit with its Wald interval and Wald P value from the conditional logistic regression (the within-category effects of 4. RUSH-era models, as the original code’s lincom, and for the Total row the model without interactions), and, once per characteristic, the interaction test of 4. RUSH-era models. Each interval the article prints matches the Wald interval worked out from its row, so these are the article’s statistics (decision issue #5). The article’s column heading, “McNemar OR”, names the odds ratio, which for paired data equals the ratio of discordant pairs; the tables here head it “OR after vs before”. The article’s χ² values fit tests with one fewer degree of freedom than categories, as the interaction test has.

The site shows the four tables with the article’s own printed values, run through the same formatting functions (Published results).

Merge years since diagnosis
Join the two by patient number. The original code used merge 1:1, which keeps every row of both files, matched or not, and then tabulated how many matched (tab _merge). full_join() keeps every row the same way. Before the join, check_unique_patients() stops if a patient number appears twice in either file, as Stata’s 1:1 does; relationship = "one-to-one" alone would check only the matched rows, so a repeated patient missing from the other file would get through.
