Scope and reporting framework
This document is the authoritative specification of the study’s objectives, population, definitions and statistical methods. ARCHITECTURE.md documents the implementation, AGENTS.md the working conventions, and GitHub Issues the open decisions and implementation status. Neither file supersedes this plan.
The study is a retrospective cohort study of routinely collected health data: laboratory, electronic medical record and Ryan White visit records. Reporting follows STROBE and RECORD (Elm et al. 2007; Benchimol et al. 2015). The reporting map at the end links each relevant checklist item to a section of this plan. Every method below is taken from the published article (Flash et al. 2015) or from the original Stata code of 15 January 2015 that produced its results (stata/RUSH_analysis_2015-01-15.do). Where the two differ, the plan says so.

1. Objective
To determine whether previously diagnosed people with HIV who were tested again in an emergency department running routine opt-out HIV testing with embedded service linkage workers, the Routine Universal Screening for HIV (RUSH) program, were more often engaged in care, retained in care and virally suppressed after the visit than before it (Flash et al. 2015).

Primary: the change from before to after the RUSH-era index visit in each of three outcomes (section 7).
Secondary: whether the change differs by sex, race and ethnicity, age, year of the visit and years since diagnosis (section 8.4); and whether the change around a RUSH-era visit is larger than the change around a visit by the same patients in the pre-RUSH era (section 8.6).
Hypothesis, stated in the article: repeated screening by the program facilitates linkage or re-linkage to HIV care for previously diagnosed patients.

2. Design
A retrospective cohort with paired before-and-after measurement: each patient’s outcomes in a period just before an emergency department visit are compared with the same outcomes just after it, so each patient serves as their own comparison. A historical comparison of the same kind, around an earlier visit by a subset of the same patients in the era before RUSH, tests whether the RUSH-era change is larger than the change around an emergency department visit without the program (Flash et al. 2015).
The design does not identify a causal effect of the program: the article notes the observational data and historical controls, and temporal changes in treatment guidelines and attention to retention (Flash et al. 2015) (section 11).

3. Data source

Setting: the Ben Taub General Hospital and Lyndon B. Johnson General Hospital emergency departments of Harris Health System, Houston, Texas, the county’s publicly funded health system (Flash et al. 2015).
HIV test records and results: electronic laboratory databases of the RUSH program, 2009 to 2012. Positive results are matched by the City of Houston Department of Health and Human Services against local and state surveillance to identify previously diagnosed cases.
Demographics, visits and viral loads: the Harris Health electronic medical record. Viral loads are available only for tests done within Harris Health.
Visits at other Ryan White funded clinics in the Houston Eligible Metropolitan Area: the Centralized Patient Care Data Management System (CPCDMS), which records the date and place of Ryan White funded visits only.
Analysis files: the cohort and outcomes were assembled before the Stata analysis into two de-identified workbooks, dated 15 January 2015: Deidentified RUSH data 1-15-2015.xlsx (sheets “Study Cohort” and “Controls”) and Deidentified Years_After_DX 1-15-2015.xlsx. Each holds one row per patient, with the outcomes already derived for the periods before and after the visit. The code that built them is not part of this repository.

4. Study population
The RUSH-era study cohort, in the order the article applies the steps (Flash et al. 2015) (Results, first paragraph; Figure 1):

HIV tests performed in the two emergency departments between 2009 and 2012 (the article reports 202,767).
Confirmed positive results (3,613), of which 2,958 were in previously diagnosed people (2,188 individuals).
Positive results from a visit at least one year after the person’s original HIV diagnosis (2,687 results), to limit confounding by recently diagnosed patients who may not yet have had time to be engaged, retained or suppressed.
The first such visit per patient: the index visit. This gives 2,068 patients.

Every patient in the “Study Cohort” sheet is analyzed; the scripts apply no further exclusion. The merge with the years-since-diagnosis workbook keeps every patient in either file, as the original code did.

5. Exposure and time zero

Exposure: an emergency department visit with an HIV test under RUSH, followed by service linkage (contact by a service linkage worker, counseling, help with eligibility, transport and appointments) (Flash et al. 2015).
Time zero: the index visit.
Covariates, each fixed at the index visit: sex; race and ethnicity; age group; calendar year of the index visit (2009 to 2012); and years from HIV diagnosis to the index visit, as a number and in five groups (5 or fewer, 6 to 10, 11 to 15, 16 to 20, more than 20). Because each is the same before and after the visit, each enters the models only through its interaction with the period (section 8.3).

6. Comparator

Within patient: the period before the index visit (section 7).
Pre-RUSH era: patients in the study cohort who had an emergency department visit in a four-year period before RUSH (the article’s example is 2004 to 2007) whose follow-up would not extend into the RUSH era, and who had been diagnosed more than one year before that visit. If a patient had several, the visit nearest to the RUSH-era index visit is used. In that era HIV testing was at the provider’s discretion, no service linkage workers worked in the emergency department, and referral to HIV care was passive (Flash et al. 2015). The article reports 672 such patients. They are a subset of the study cohort and carry the same patient number in the “Controls” sheet.

7. Outcomes
Each outcome is measured in a window before and a window after the visit (Flash et al. 2015) (Methods, “Data Sources and Analysis”):

Engagement in care: at least one HIV primary care visit in the 6 months before, and in the 6 months after, the visit. The article calls this “engagement” rather than “linkage” because the patients were not newly diagnosed.
Retention in care: the HRSA definition, two HIV primary care visits at least 3 months apart in the 12 months before, and in the 12 months after, the visit.
Viral suppression: an HIV viral load below 200 copies/mL at any time in the 12 months before, and the 12 months after, the visit. Because a viral load drawn within days of the visit reflects care before it, the before window runs to 10 days after the visit, and the after window from day 11 to 12 months and 10 days after it.

Primary analysis: a patient with no viral load result in a window counts as not suppressed.
Secondary analysis: a patient with no result in a window is missing for that window. Only patients with a result in both windows inform the paired comparison.


Visits count if they appear in the Harris Health record or in CPCDMS. In the workbooks each care outcome is 0 or 1 for each window, and viral load is the text “Suppressed” or “Not Suppressed”, or empty.

8. Statistical analysis

8.1 Data structure
One record per patient and window: the before and after values of each outcome form a matched pair, and in the era comparison a patient with a visit in both eras contributes two pairs.


8.2 Overall change
The proportion of patients with each outcome before and after the index visit, compared with McNemar’s test for paired proportions (McNemar 1947; Flash et al. 2015). The original code ran McNemar’s test for engagement and retention only, with the comment that it was there to confirm the conditional logistic regression (section 8.3) gives the same results. The article’s Methods describe McNemar’s test for all three outcomes; the code does not record where the viral suppression P value came from.

Open: whether the R version should add McNemar’s test for viral suppression, as the article’s Methods describe, or keep the original code’s set (decision issue #3).



8.3 Conditional logistic regression
Each outcome is modelled with conditional logistic regression, with one stratum per patient, the outcome as the dependent variable and an indicator for the period after the visit (post_visit) as the main term (Flash et al. 2015). Conditioning on the patient removes every characteristic that does not change between the two windows. The exponentiated post_visit coefficient is the conditional odds ratio for the outcome after the visit compared with before it. The exact conditional likelihood is used, as Stata’s clogit uses.


8.4 Differences by patient characteristics
For each characteristic in section 5, and each outcome, a conditional logistic regression with post_visit and its interaction with the characteristic (Flash et al. 2015):

Test of difference: a joint Wald test that every interaction coefficient is zero (Stata’s testparm).
Effect within each category: the odds ratio for post_visit in each category, from the sum of the post_visit coefficient and that category’s interaction coefficient (Stata’s lincom).
Race and ethnicity in four groups: Black, Hispanic, White, and other (the original code labels it “Asian/Other/Unknown”); the article’s Methods name the groups White non-Hispanic, Black non-Hispanic, Hispanic and other. The original code also tested race as recorded, and an African American indicator.
Years since diagnosis and age together: one model with both interactions, to see whether a difference by years since diagnosis remains once age is allowed for (original code).
Not fitted: the interaction of race as recorded with viral suppression (missing excluded), which the original code could not fit.

The reference category is the first in the original code’s order: the earliest year (2009); 5 or fewer years since diagnosis; and, for sex, age group and race, the first value in alphabetical order of the recorded text (Stata’s encode numbering).


8.5 Multivariable models
For engagement, retention and viral suppression (missing as not suppressed), a conditional logistic regression with post_visit and its interactions with year of visit, sex, age group and the African American indicator; and the same with race as recorded in place of the indicator (original code). The abstract’s “multivariate conditional logistic regression” refers to these models; the article does not tabulate them.


8.6 Comparison with the pre-RUSH era
The two cohorts are stacked: up to four records per patient (before and after each era’s visit). A conditional logistic regression with one stratum per patient includes (Flash et al. 2015):

post_visit: the change around a pre-RUSH visit;
rush_era: the difference between the periods before each era’s visit;
post_visit × rush_era: whether the change around the visit differs between the eras, as a ratio of odds ratios. Its P value is the one the article reports for each outcome.

The original code also fitted, for sex, age group and race in four groups, the same model with every term interacted with the characteristic, testing all the interaction terms jointly; and, for comparison, a random-intercept logistic model in place of the strata (Stata’s xtlogit, adaptive quadrature with 12 points) (Bates et al. 2015). Year of visit is not used: it cannot overlap between eras. With every patient, two three-way models could not be fitted (race groups with viral suppression, missing as not suppressed; race groups with retention) and are not fitted.
The original code fitted every era model twice: first with every patient, including those with a RUSH-era visit only (its comment says this was done “by request”), and then with only the patients with a visit in both eras.

Open: which of the two samples produced the P values the article reports for the era comparison (decision issue #2).



8.7 Missing data
Missing viral load results are handled as in section 7.3. The care outcomes are used as recorded in the workbook; a patient missing one in a window drops out of the comparisons of that outcome. Patients missing a characteristic are left out of the models that use it.


8.8 Multiplicity and significance
No adjustment for multiple comparisons. P < 0.05 is significant.


8.9 Software
The published analysis used Stata 12 and SPSS 21 (Flash et al. 2015); the Stata code is in stata/. The article’s Tables 1 to 4 are not made by the Stata code; the R version builds them (R/tables.R, with gtsummary): Table 1 as counts and percentages by cohort, and Tables 2 to 4 as, for each subgroup, the numbers before and after, the odds ratio for the visit with its Wald 95% confidence interval and Wald P value from the conditional logistic regression, and the interaction test of section 8.4 across the subgroup’s categories. The odds ratio for each category comes from the model with the visit-by-characteristic interaction (section 8.4, as the original code’s lincom) and the Total row from the model with the visit alone (section 8.3), so every row of a table is on the same footing; these are the statistics the article prints (decision issue #5). A category in which no patient’s outcome got worse has an infinite odds ratio and no P value, printed “∞” and “-” as in the article’s Table 4. The tables run no McNemar test. Mean age is not computed: the workbooks hold age groups only. The R version uses survival::clogit() (Therneau, n.d.) and lme4::glmer() (Bates et al. 2015).

9. Sensitivity analyses

Viral load missing as missing (section 7.3), against the primary analysis in which missing counts as not suppressed. It tests the assumption that a patient without a Harris Health viral load was not suppressed.
Era comparison with every patient or only those with both eras (section 8.6).
Random-intercept models (section 8.6), which also use differences between patients and assume the patient effect is unrelated to the visit and era.

10. Disclosure control
The workbooks are de-identified patient-level data of Harris Health System and are not published in this repository. Only numbers reported in the article are quoted, with their location in the article. Nothing computed from the study data is committed.

title: Clinical background
text:
The HIV care continuum
Diagnosis is only the first step. A person with HIV benefits, and stops transmitting the virus to sexual partners, only if they are linked to HIV care, stay in care, take antiretroviral therapy and reach a suppressed viral load. Each step loses people. The RUSH article cites national estimates that about one in five people aware of their HIV had not been linked to care, and that only about half of those linked were retained (Flash et al. 2015). People who fall out of care are hard to find: they are, by definition, no longer coming to the clinic.

title: Clinical background
text:
Why previously diagnosed patients matter
A routine testing program in the emergency department tests everyone who does not decline, so it tests again many people who already know they have HIV, including some who do not mention it and some who have dropped out of care. Retesting them is usually seen as waste. The RUSH investigators asked the opposite question: if the program is paired with staff whose job is to link every positive patient to care, is retesting a previously diagnosed patient an opportunity to bring them back? (Flash et al. 2015)

title: Clinical background
text:
The RUSH program
Harris Health System is the publicly funded health system of Harris County, Texas; most of its patients have no other coverage. It started the Routine Universal Screening for HIV (RUSH) program in 2008, following the CDC recommendations, adding an HIV test for every patient 16 or older having blood drawn or an IV placed unless they opted out. The program began in the Ben Taub General Hospital emergency department and reached the Lyndon B. Johnson General Hospital emergency department in 2009 (Flash et al. 2015).
The key ingredient for previously diagnosed patients is the service linkage worker. Based in each emergency department, they contact every patient who tests positive (the next business day for tests done at night or at weekends), deliver results, and help with what keeps people from care: eligibility paperwork for Harris Health and Ryan White services, the AIDS Drug Assistance Program, transport, and appointments. A patient stays on their caseload until they have seen an HIV provider, and is then handed to a service linkage worker at the HIV clinic, who helps with retention. Before RUSH, HIV testing in these departments was at the treating provider’s discretion, and patients were referred to HIV care passively, with a phone number (Flash et al. 2015).
Outpatient HIV care in the system is given mainly at Thomas Street Health Center, the oldest free-standing HIV clinic in the United States, and two satellite clinics. Some patients receive care at other Ryan White funded clinics in Houston, which is why the study also used the Houston area’s shared Ryan White visit database (Flash et al. 2015).

title: Clinical background
text:
The three outcomes
The study measured three steps of the care continuum, each before and after the emergency department visit (Flash et al. 2015):

Engagement in care: an HIV primary care visit within 6 months. For a newly diagnosed person this would be called linkage; for people diagnosed earlier the article calls it engagement.
Retention in care: two HIV primary care visits at least 3 months apart within 12 months, the HRSA measure.
Viral suppression: a viral load below 200 copies/mL within 12 months.

How each is measured, and why the viral load windows are shifted by 10 days, is on Study design and methods.

Data flow

Key mechanisms

Within-patient models. Every conditional model goes through fit_conditional_logit(), which adds strata(patient_number) and uses the exact conditional likelihood. In 04, characteristics appear only in interactions with post_visit; in 05 the subgroup models are the full factorial post_visit * rush_era * characteristic, since a characteristic can differ between a patient’s eras. fit_conditional_logit() fits to complete rows from patients whose outcome varies, with categories then empty dropped, as Stata’s clogit drops uninformative groups; reference levels therefore follow the estimation sample, and effect_by_level() lists dropped categories as not estimable.
Stata’s category numbering. encode_like_stata() orders factor levels by byte order, so reference levels match the original code’s encode. clean_cohort() applies it to race, sex and age group in both sheets.
Race groups from codes, per sheet. group_race_codes() maps race_code to race_group with race_group_codes_study or race_group_codes_control (setup.R); 02 prints the code-to-value table. The stacked data use race_group, sex and age group as text-labelled factors, never codes.
Reported quantities. effect_by_level() (Stata’s lincom) and wald_test() (Stata’s testparm) work from model_coefficients(), which handles both clogit() and glmer() models. Interaction coefficient names come from interaction_terms(), built from model$xlevels, so they match exactly.
Results in nested named lists. Repeated fits are for-loops over names into lists indexed [[characteristic]][[outcome]], or [[sample]][[outcome]] in 05.
Skipped models in one place. skipped_rush_subgroup_models and skipped_era_subgroup_models_all (setup.R) list the models the original code could not fit; 04 and 05 skip them by lookup.
Two era samples. era_samples holds all_patients and both_eras (patients with rows_per_patient_both_eras rows); every model in 05 loops over both.
One layout for computed and published tables. format_table_1() and format_outcome_table() take rows of text, so R/tables.R (from the data) and the published-results page (from the article’s printed values in quarto/published/) produce tables with the same layout.
Inputs are checked. 01 stops if RUSH_DATA_DIR is unset or a workbook lacks an expected column; the message names columns only. check_unique_patients() stops the import if a patient number repeats in any sheet.

Dependencies outside this repository

The study data, in the folder named by RUSH_DATA_DIR: the two de-identified workbooks. Neither is in the repository; their columns have not been checked against the code.
Packages attached in setup.R: tidyverse, readxl, survival, lme4 and gtsummary (with gt to save the tables). The synthetic test also needs writexl.

Website
Each definitive script has a page in quarto/ that imports its labelled sections with knitr::read_chunk() and shows them without running them. quarto/_stata_sections.R reads stata/RUSH_analysis_2015-01-15.do as text and splits it into 29 parts, each starting at one of the file’s own comment lines (it stops if an anchor is missing); quarto/original_stata.qmd shows every part with a link to its R page, and each script page shows its parts in folded boxes beside the R that replaces them. .github/workflows/publish.yml renders the site and publishes it to gh-pages.

Tests
tests/synthetic/build_synthetic_data.R writes random workbooks with the expected sheets, columns and value formats. tests/synthetic/run_pipeline.R runs R/main.R on them and checks that: the conditional odds ratio for paired data equals the ratio of discordant pairs; effect_by_level() equals a model fitted within each age group; wald_test() equals survival’s Wald test and the squared z statistic; every interaction test found its coefficients; the era subgroup model equals the full-factorial model, with the age main effect estimated; the restricted era sample has four rows per patient; paired_mcnemar() equals mcnemar.test(); the interval for the visit is the Wald interval of the discordant pairs and the Total row of Table 2 shows it; and, on small invented data, that a category in which no patient got worse prints “∞” and “-”, that a category with only uninformative patients is reported as not estimable with the others correctly labelled, that repeated patient numbers stop the import, that McNemar’s test without discordant pairs returns missing values; and that the four tables are built and saved. .github/workflows/test-pipeline.yml runs it on every pull request.
